body:
D'var Torah on Parshas VaEira: Leadership, Listening, and the Jewish Eye for Detail

Introduction: The Book of Names and Identity

Baruch Hashem, here we are on Erev Shabbos, continuing our journey through Sefer Shemos, the Sefer of Names. This sefer is not only about events, it is about identity. It teaches us who we are as Jewish people and what it truly means to be a Jew.

The very name of the sefer tells us this. "Shemos" means names, and names matter. The Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 32:5) teaches that the Jewish people were redeemed from Egypt because they maintained three things: their names, their language, and their clothing. They held onto their identity even in exile.

The Genealogy: Leadership Has Roots

In Parshas VaEira, the Torah pauses the narrative to give us the genealogy of Moshe and Aharon, their yichus. The Torah says (Shemos 6:14): "אלה ראשי בית אבתם," these are the heads of their fathers' houses. Then it continues (Shemos 6:16): "ואלה שמות בני לוי לתולדתם," and these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations.

The Torah is reminding us that leadership does not appear out of nowhere. It grows through continuity, transmission, and character over time. There is lineage, there are named fathers going back generations. These are real people, not mythological heroes.

Rashi comments on this genealogy, explaining that the Torah traces the lineage specifically to show us who Moshe and Aharon truly are. They come from somewhere. They carry the legacy of those who came before them.

Yet lineage alone is not enough. To understand Moshe and Aharon, we must step further back and look at Levi himself.

Levi: The Power of Listening

Levi was not the bechor, the firstborn. He was not the youngest. He was not singled out as a favorite. So what made him special?

We return to the episode of Shechem (Bereishis 34). When Dinah was violated, Levi stepped forward with Shimon to defend his sister's honor. The Torah records (Bereishis 34:25): "ויקחו שני בני יעקב שמעון ולוי אחי דינה איש חרבו," And two of Yaakov's sons, Shimon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his sword.

They acted with strength, with courage, with righteous indignation. But what defines Levi most is not the act itself, it is what follows.

When Yaakov rebukes them at the end of his life, saying (Bereishis 49:5-7): "שמעון ולוי אחים כלי חמס מכרתיהם... ארור אפם כי עז," Shimon and Levi are brothers, instruments of violence are their weapons... Cursed be their anger for it is fierce, Levi does not argue. He does not justify himself. He listens.

This ability to receive tochacha, rebuke, is rare. It requires humility and trust. Levi understands that his father sees truth as well, even when that truth is painful.

The contrast with Shimon is instructive. Shimon's descendants receive no independent portion in Eretz Yisrael. But Levi's descendants? They become the teachers, the Kohanim, the spiritual leaders of the nation. Why? Because Levi was able to buckle himself, to sit back and receive correction without defensiveness.

Pirkei Avos (4:1) describes this quality succinctly: "איזהו חכם הלומד מכל אדם," Who is wise? One who learns from every person. Leadership begins not with authority, but with listening.

Transmitting Middos: The Chain of Character

As a father, Levi would naturally want to pass this quality on to his children, not only through instruction, but through personal example. As parents, we understand this instinctively. Our children do not only absorb what we teach them, they absorb how we respond to correction. Our children reflect us. Their behaviors, their mannerisms, their instincts come from what we model and what we actively teach.

The Gemara in Berachos (58a) teaches about seeing a large gathering of Jews: "ברוך חכם הרזים שאין דעתם דומה זה לזה ואין פרצופיהן דומים זה לזה," Blessed is the Knower of secrets, for their minds are not similar to one another and their faces are not similar to one another. Yet there is also transmission, a passing down of core values and middos from generation to generation.

Levi did the same for his sons, and their sons, eventually leading to Moshe and Aharon. The Torah traces this explicitly: Levi to Kehat (Shemos 6:16), from Kehat to Amram (Shemos 6:18), and from Amram to Moshe and Aharon (Shemos 6:20).

This ability to listen, to be mekabel tochacha, while at the same time having the confidence to stand up for what is right, as Levi did in Shechem, is a core leadership quality. This quality was passed down through the generations to Moshe and to Aharon.

Moshe and Aharon become leaders who listen: to Hashem, to the people, and to each other.

Running From Honor

Pirkei Avos (6:5) also teaches: "כל הבורח מן הכבוד הכבוד רודף אחריו," One who runs away from honor, honor pursues him. Levi never seeks prominence. He withdraws from power struggles. After the incident in Shechem, he does not seek recognition or vindication. Leadership comes to him naturally, through his descendants.

This is not coincidence. It is Torah psychology, the way Hashem designed the world to work.

Moshe himself exemplifies this. When Hashem appears to him at the burning bush, Moshe resists. He says (Shemos 4:13): "בי ה' שלח נא ביד תשלח," Please, Hashem, send through whomever You will send. He does not want the position. And precisely because of that, he is the right person for it.

The Universal Message: Leadership for All

At this point, we might ask ourselves: do we need to be Leviim for this message to apply? Most of us are not from the tribe of Levi.

The Rambam (Hilchos Shemittah V'Yovel 13:13) answers clearly: "ולא שבט לוי בלבד אלא כל איש ואיש מכל באי העולם אשר נדבה רוחו אותו," Not only the tribe of Levi, but any person from all who come into the world whose spirit moves them to stand before Hashem to serve Him. Leadership rooted in responsibility, in service, is open to all.

At this stage in history, generations later, we all carry something of every shevet within us. We have a bit of Levi, a bit of Shimon, Yehudah, Naftali, Dan, all of them. The qualities of the tribes are part of our collective inheritance.

So what does it mean to be a Jew today? Where does leadership come from? In life, we receive messages, and we receive messengers. We must be willing to open our ears and listen.

In the previous parsha, we saw the passphrase Hashem gave to Moshe to present to the zekeinim (Shemos 3:16): "פקד פקדתי אתכם," I have surely remembered you. This was a sign, passed down from the Avos, that he was truly sent. Leadership and truth are recognized through consistency and integrity, not just lineage.

The Makos Begin: Lessons for Us

Parshas VaEira brings us into the makos, the plagues. The Torah introduces them with a purpose statement (Shemos 7:5): "וידעו מצרים כי אני ה'," And Egypt shall know that I am Hashem. But the makos are not only for Pharaoh and Egypt, they are for us. The Torah says multiple times "למען תדע," so that you will know.

The makos serve two purposes. One is to teach Pharaoh and the world. The other is to teach us, to remind us of Hashem's presence and reality.

The First Mako: Water to Blood

The first mako turns water into blood. The Torah describes (Shemos 7:20): "ויך את המים אשר ביאור ויהפכו כל המים אשר ביאור לדם," And he struck the water that was in the river, and all the water that was in the river turned to blood.

Egypt's power was built on the Nile. The Egyptians worshiped the Nile as a deity. When it collapses, their illusion collapses with it. The very source of their strength becomes their weakness.

For the Jews, water remained water. They simply had to relate correctly to dam, to blood. The lesson is not destruction, but correct relationship.

Blood already had deep meaning in Jewish life. In the times of the Beis HaMikdash, blood was treated with precision and reverence in the avodah of korbanos. In shechitah, it is not only about removal of blood, but also about respect for it. The Torah commands (Vayikra 17:13): "וכסהו בעפר," And he shall cover it with earth, when slaughtering certain animals.

This theme returns again at the climax of the makos, with the blood on the doorposts (Shemos 12:7). Blood that protects, blood that sanctifies, blood that carries meaning.

Water is something we take for granted. The human body is mostly water. The world is largely water. We need it to live. But when we treat it as a god, when we abuse our relationship with it, it can turn against us. Mitzrayim depended on water and abused it. When it was taken from them, their reality collapsed.

The Mako of Lice: The Finger of God

The mako of kinim, lice, marks a turning point. This is the third mako, and the Torah records (Shemos 8:15): "ויאמרו החרטמים אל פרעה אצבע אלקים הוא," And the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God."

The Egyptian magicians finally admit defeat. They could replicate the first two makos using their sorcery, but not this one. Why?

Chazal explain (Sanhedrin 67b) that they could not recreate it because it was too small, too precise. Something so tiny, smaller than a grain of barley, was beyond their power. It was too exact. Only Hashem could create life from dust.

This reflects the Jewish approach to life. Even the smallest details matter. Judaism lives in the details.

Halacha deals in measurements. The Gemara in Eruvin discusses minimum sizes for everything: the size of an olive (k'zayis), the size of an egg (k'beitzah), the size of a date (k'koteves). Sometimes something smaller than a minimum size is halachically irrelevant. Other times, even something extremely small, like a visible insect on lettuce, carries full halachic weight and must be addressed.

Why? Because Hashem is present even in the smallest actions. We live in the details because Hashem is found in the details. Even the smallest actions are under Hashem's ratzon, Hashem's will.

The Baal Shem Tov teaches that nothing happens by chance. Every movement of a leaf, every flutter of a butterfly's wing, is guided by Divine Providence. How much more so the details of our mitzvos, our relationships, our words?

Moshe and Hakaras HaTov: Eternal Gratitude

This brings us back to Moshe Rabbeinu and one of the most beautiful teachings in the parsha.

When the Nile must be struck for the makos of blood and frogs, Moshe does not do it. Aharon does. The Torah specifically records (Shemos 7:19): "ויאמר ה' אל משה אמר אל אהרן," And Hashem said to Moshe: Say to Aharon. Why doesn't Moshe do it himself?

Rashi explains beautifully: "לפי שהגן עליו כשנשלך לתוכו לפיכך לא לקה על ידו," Because the river protected him when he was cast into it, therefore it was not struck by his hand.

This is hakaras hatov, gratitude that never expires. Even decades later, even when Hashem Himself commands the action, Moshe remembers. The river that saved his life as a baby deserves his respect.

Chazal express this principle (Bava Kamma 92b): "לא תזרוק אבן בבאר ששתית ממנו מים," Do not throw a stone into a well from which you drank. Even an inanimate object that benefited you deserves recognition.

This teaches us how a Jew looks at the world. Everything is a creation of Hashem. When something benefits us, we respond with appreciation, not worship, but respect. We recognize its role and its purpose.

I appreciate my car because it serves a purpose. I do not abuse it. I recognize its role. How much more so must we show gratitude to people who have helped us, taught us, supported us?

The Gemara in Shabbos (31a) teaches that one of the first questions we will be asked in the World to Come is: "נשאת ונתת באמונה," Did you conduct your business faithfully? This includes faithfulness to our commitments, to our word, and to our gratitude.

Aharon, who did not have that same direct relationship with the river, was able to strike it when Hashem commanded it. This too is yashrus, straightness. This is knowing when gratitude yields to obligation, when different values come into proper balance.

The Jewish Approach: Living in the Details

Parshas VaEira teaches us how to live as Jews. To listen before speaking. To lead without chasing leadership. To notice the small things that others miss. To carry gratitude for a lifetime, never forgetting those who have helped us.

Every word of Torah, every letter, every nekudah exists to help us build a relationship with Hashem and to understand what it truly means to be a Jew.

The Ramban in his introduction to Sefer Shemos explains that this entire sefer is about the building of the Jewish people as a nation. Not just physically leaving Egypt, but becoming who we are meant to be: a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

The Message for Our Lives

Leadership is not about power or position. It is about character, humility, and the ability to listen. It is passed down through generations, modeled more than taught.

Attention to detail is not pedantry. It is recognizing that Hashem is present in everything, that nothing is beneath our notice or care.

Gratitude is not a feeling that fades. It is a commitment, a way of seeing the world that honors every person, every creature, every object that has served us.

These are the foundations of a Jewish life. These are what make us who we are.

Reflection and Growth

As we prepare for Shabbos, consider these questions:

On Listening and Leadership:

When was the last time I received criticism or rebuke? How did I respond? Did I listen, or did I defend?

Do I seek leadership positions, or do I focus on serving and let leadership come naturally?

On Generational Transmission:

What middos am I actively working to pass down to the next generation?

Do my children see me modeling the values I claim to hold, or only hear me teaching them?

On Attention to Detail:

Do I rush through mitzvos, or do I pay attention to the small details that make them meaningful?

Do I see Hashem's hand in the small moments of my day, or only in the big events?

On Gratitude:

Who are the people, living or deceased, who have helped shape who I am? Have I expressed gratitude to them?

Is there someone from my past who helped me that I've forgotten to thank?

Closing Thought

The journey from Levi to Moshe and Aharon is not just a genealogy. It is a map of how character builds over generations, how listening creates leaders, and how gratitude shapes a people.

As we enter Shabbos, may we merit to listen more deeply, to notice more carefully, to appreciate more fully. May we be part of the chain that passes these values forward, building not just our own lives, but the future of Klal Yisrael.

Every detail matters. Every act of gratitude counts. Every moment of listening builds leadership.

This is what it means to be a Jew.

Have a wonderful Shabbos.
